app.setup.title: Set up Clotr
app.setup.lead: Clotr is a keyboard. Turn it on, then pick it, and it starts checking what you type in AI apps.
app.setup.androidWarns: Android will warn you that Clotr may collect all the text you type. It shows that warning for every keyboard, not only this one.
app.setup.whyNotSend: Clotr can't send anything anywhere: it has no permission to use the internet. Settings, under What Clotr stores, shows you where to check.
app.setup.reads: It reads the message box of AI apps on its list while you type with it. In other apps it's an ordinary keyboard until you switch Clotr on there yourself. It skips password boxes.
app.setup.keeps: It keeps your settings on this phone, the scrambled codes of the details you asked it to protect, and a history of what it found: the time, the app, the kind of detail, what you chose. Never what you typed.
app.setup.learns: It learns the words you type in ordinary text fields, not passwords, PINs, numbers, email addresses or web addresses, encrypted on this phone. Turn it off, or tap Forget my words, any time in Settings.
app.setup.noAI: It keeps no clipboard history and has no AI inside.
app.setup.sendsNowhere: It sends nothing anywhere. Android won't let it go online, and your phone's backups leave it out.
app.setup.howToStop: To stop, tap the keyboard button at the bottom of the screen to switch back, or turn it off in Settings, System, Keyboard.

app.planSeedWhat: Move the money in this crypto wallet to a new wallet, then delete the file.
app.planSeedWhy: A wallet's seed words are the wallet itself. Anyone who reads them can take everything in it, and changing a password doesn't stop that.
app.planSeedHowSteps: Open the file with the button below so you know which wallet the words belong to. / In your wallet app, make a brand new wallet. Write its new seed words on paper and keep them somewhere private, never in a photo, a note or a file. / Send everything from the old wallet to the new one, and check it arrived before you go on. / Once the old wallet is empty, press Delete on the file below and confirm when your phone asks. / If you also kept a photo or screenshot of the old words, delete it too, then empty the trash in Google Photos or Files.
app.planKeysHowSteps: Open the file with the button below and find which account, site or app each password or key belongs to. / Open that account's own app or website, sign in, and look for Change password or Security. / Set a new password there, then do the same for every other one in the file. / Once they're all changed, press Delete on the file below and confirm when your phone asks. / A password manager keeps them all behind one password, so none sit in a plain file again. Most Android phones come with Google Password Manager. Search for Passwords in your phone's Settings to find it.
app.planIdPhotosHowSteps: Open the photo with the button below so you know which one it is. / If you still need it, open Google Photos, open the photo, tap the three dots and choose Move to Locked Folder. It stays behind your screen lock and out of your backups. / The Files by Google app has a locked folder of its own, under Collections, that only opens with your PIN. On a Samsung phone, open Settings and search for folder to find Samsung's own locked one. / If you don't need it on your phone, press Delete below and confirm when your phone asks. Check Google Photos too, since it may keep a backup copy.
app.planIdDocsHowSteps: Open the file with the button below and find the number in it. / If you still need the number, keep it somewhere only you can open, like a password manager with room for notes, or on paper at home. / Press Delete on the file below and confirm when your phone asks. / If the file came to you in a chat or an email, it's probably still there too. Delete it there as well if you don't need it.
app.planPhotoPlaceHowSteps: Tap a photo below and choose Remove the place, keep the photo. Clotr takes out where it was taken and leaves the picture as it was. / If Clotr can't change the original, it saves a cleaned copy in your Pictures. Check the copy, then delete the original. / To stop new photos saving the place, open your Camera app's settings and turn off Save location. Some phones call it Location tags.
app.planMoneyHowSteps: Open the file with the button below and find the card or bank number in it. / If it's a card you still use and you've shared the file, call your bank or use its app to ask for a new card. / If you still need the number, keep it in a password manager with room for notes, not in a file. / Press Delete on the file below and confirm when your phone asks.
app.planLeaveOutHowSteps: Tap a file below and choose Leave this folder out. Clotr stops looking in that folder from the next scan on, and never touches the files in it. / To change your mind later, open Settings and find Leave out of scans, where each folder has its own Remove button.

app.results.askHelpLead: Print or share a note with what Clotr found, for someone to look at with you.
app.noteMeta: Made by Clotr for Android on this phone, $1, from $2.
app.noteIntro: Clotr looked through this phone and found a few files worth your help. None of it is an emergency, and nothing has been sent anywhere. Here is what it found, worst first, and what it suggests.
app.noteIs: Clotr is a free app that looks through the files on a person's phone for passwords, ID photos and numbers, card and bank numbers, and photos that show where they were taken. It runs only on the phone and sends nothing anywhere. This note lists what it found and what it suggests, so you can explain it and help with the steps. It names kinds of detail and places, never the details themselves, and it leaves file names out unless the person chose to include them.
app.noteFooter: Clotr made this note on the person's phone. It was printed or shared by them; Clotr itself sends nothing anywhere.
app.noteStepsKeys: Open the file in Clotr's results and see which account, site or app each password or key belongs to. / Sign in to that account and look for Change password or Security. / Set a new password, and do the same for every other one in the file. / Back in Clotr, delete the file.
app.noteStepsIdPhotos: Open the photo in Clotr's results to see which one it is. / If it's still needed, move it to a locked folder, like Google Photos' Locked Folder or the Files by Google app's own one. / If it isn't needed on the phone, delete it in Clotr, and check apps like Google Photos for a backup copy too.
app.noteStepsPhotoPlace: Open the photo in Clotr's results and choose Remove the place. Clotr takes out where it was taken and keeps the photo itself.

Windows doesn't come with one built in, so you'd need to choose and set one up yourself.
ws.planIdPhotosHowSteps: Open the photo with the button below so you know which file you're moving. / If you already use OneDrive, open it in File Explorer, find Personal Vault in the list on the left, and move the photo in there. This locks the folder to your own Windows sign-in, though it only works on Windows 11 Pro, Enterprise or Education, which leaves out Home, and it's worth backing up the certificate it offers to make, since a forgotten sign-in can lock you out of the folder for good. / If you don't need the photo on this PC at all, right click it, choose Delete, then empty the Recycle Bin.
